clinicalPearls: AVRT is a macroreentrant tachycardia that obligatorily uses an accessory atrioventricular pathway as one limb and the AV node as the other.

Orthodromic AVRT conducts antegradely through the AV node and retrogradely up the accessory pathway, producing a narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave typically after the QRS (RP shorter than PR).
Antidromic AVRT conducts antegradely down the accessory pathway and retrogradely through the node, giving a wide, maximally pre-excited QRS that can mimic ventricular tachycardia.
A concealed accessory pathway conducts only retrogradely, so the resting ECG is normal and pre-excitation is absent despite recurrent orthodromic tachycardia.
QRS alternans and a rate that slows with functional bundle branch block ipsilateral to the pathway (Coumel sign) point to AVRT over AVNRT.
Adenosine and vagal manoeuvres terminate orthodromic AVRT by blocking the nodal limb of the circuit.
In patients with an antegradely conducting pathway, atrial fibrillation can conduct rapidly to the ventricle and degenerate into ventricular fibrillation, so AV-nodal blocking drugs are hazardous.
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is highly effective and is first-line for symptomatic or high-risk patients.
reference.pathophysiology: AVRT depends on an accessory pathway, a strand of working myocardium that bridges the atrioventricular groove outside the normal conduction axis and electrically connects atrium to ventricle. This creates the potential for a large reentrant loop in which the impulse travels down one connection and up the other. In orthodromic tachycardia the AV node and His-Purkinje system form the antegrade limb and the accessory pathway the retrograde limb, yielding a narrow QRS. In antidromic tachycardia the direction reverses and the ventricle is activated entirely through the pathway, producing a fully pre-excited wide complex. Pathways may conduct in both directions, only antegradely, or only retrogradely (concealed). The circuit is initiated by a premature beat that blocks in one limb and returns through the other once refractoriness has resolved.
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG in sinus rhythm to seek a delta wave and short PR interval
twelve-lead ECG during tachycardia to define RP relationship and QRS alternans
transthoracic echocardiography to exclude Ebstein anomaly and other structural disease
electrophysiological study to localise the pathway and assess its antegrade refractory period
exercise testing to evaluate abrupt loss of pre-excitation suggesting a low-risk pathway
ambulatory monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm
redFlags: pre-excited atrial fibrillation with very short RR intervals indicating risk of ventricular fibrillation
wide-complex tachycardia that is haemodynamically unstable
family history of sudden cardiac death with ventricular pre-excitation
administration of AV-nodal blockers precipitating haemodynamic collapse in pre-excited AF
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent when the pathway lacks rapid antegrade conduction, and catheter ablation provides a durable cure in most patients. The principal risk is sudden death from pre-excited atrial fibrillation degenerating to ventricular fibrillation in those with a rapidly conducting antegrade pathway.
pitfalls: Giving atrioventricular nodal blocking agents to a patient with pre-excited atrial fibrillation and accelerating ventricular response.
Misdiagnosing antidromic AVRT as ventricular tachycardia and withholding appropriate management.
Assuming a normal resting ECG excludes an accessory pathway, missing a concealed pathway.
Underestimating risk in asymptomatic pre-excitation without electrophysiological risk stratification.
Failing to recognise QRS alternans and Coumel sign as clues that favour AVRT over AVNRT.
